progression.prerequisiteKnowledge: chem-m6-c12 (titration, standard solution, primary standard, aliquot, burette, titrant, titre, indicator, endpoint, equivalence point, rough and concordant titres within 0.10 mL, the four steps "known to moles, ratio, unknown", Na₂CO₃ + 2HCl, sodium carbonate dried before weighing). chem-m6-p04 and p05 (volumetric pipette and flask used in a dilution; the pipette filler). chem-m5-p01 (validity, reliability, accuracy; variables; risk). Year 11 (n = m/M, n = cV). Not assumed: rinsing rules, meniscus reading, bubbles, error direction.
progression.startsWith: Prepare or select a standard, then set up burette and pipette. The video opens: Two lab benches titrate the same hydrochloric acid against the same standard. Each bench's titres agree within zero point zero five millilitres. But bench A's average is twenty four point three three, and bench B's is twenty four point eight two.
progression.stopsAfter: preparing a sodium carbonate standard and explaining each step; calculating its concentration; pipetting an aliquot and explaining the rinse, the filler and the last drop; explaining why the conical flask may be wet; setting up and reading a burette to 0.05 mL at eye level, with no tip bubble; carrying out a rough run and accurate runs to the first permanent orange; recording a titre table, excluding a faulty run for a known cause and repeating it; calculating the unknown concentration; tracing a technique error through the titre to the answer; naming the controlled conditions; judging validity, reliability and accuracy, including why concordant titres can still be inaccurate; writing the risk rows. No indicator choice (chem-m6-c13), no error-direction tables (chem-m6-g04), no aliquot scale-up or percentage by mass (chem-m6-g03), no percentage uncertainty.
progression.nextLesson: standardisation and titration calculation practice (route chem-m6-g03).

teaching.task: Two benches titrate the same hydrochloric acid against the same standard. Both get concordant titres, but their means differ by half a millilitre. How do you carry out a titration step by step so the titre can be trusted, and how do you trace what went wrong?
teaching.causalExplanation: (1) concordant titres on both benches, different means: which is right? (1); (2) the plan: a weighed standard in the flask, the unknown in the burette, carbonate takes two HCl (C12) (2); (3) dry the solid so none of its mass is water; weigh exactly; rinse every grain into the flask (3); (4) make up to the mark and invert so every aliquot is the same; the standard's concentration from its mass (4); (5) rinse the pipette with the carbonate because water would dilute it; leave the last drop because the pipette is calibrated that way; the flask can be wet because water adds no moles (5); (6) rinse the burette with the acid; remove the funnel; fill the tip so no bubble is counted as acid (6); (7) read at eye level to 0.05 mL; the numbers get bigger going down, so a reading from above is too low (7); (8) a rough run finds the endpoint; accurate runs go dropwise near it, to the first permanent orange (8); (9) titre = final − initial; a run with a known fault (a bubble) is excluded and repeated; mean of three concordant titres (9); (10) the calculation (10); (11) bench B: water in the burette dilutes the acid, so more millilitres react with the same carbonate, the titre is too big and the answer too low; rinse with what's going in (11); controlled conditions (12); validity, reliability, accuracy (13); risk (14); attempts and brief feedback (15 to 18); decision rule and handoff (19); key notes (20).
teaching.conversationalApproach: two benches titrate the same acid against the same standard and both get concordant titres, yet their means differ by half a millilitre, so the practical asks how to carry out each step so a titre can be trusted and how to trace what went wrong. The plan puts a weighed sodium carbonate standard in the flask and the unknown hydrochloric acid in the burette; each step then gets its reason: dry, weigh and rinse every grain in, make up to the mark and invert, rinse the pipette and burette with what goes in, clear the tip bubble, read the meniscus at eye level, titrate a rough run first and then drop by drop. Bench A's table drops the run with a recorded fault, the C12 calculation is staged one line per stage, and bench B's water-rinsed burette is traced through the titre to a concentration that comes out too low. Controlled conditions, validity, reliability and accuracy, and the risk assessment follow. Two exam questions follow with brief feedback.
teaching.openingDecision: Two lab benches titrate the same hydrochloric acid against the same standard. Each bench's titres agree within zero point zero five millilitres. But bench A's average is twenty four point three three, and bench B's is twenty four point eight two. So how do you run a titration you can trust, and spot what went wrong?
teaching.understandingCheck: (A1) "A student rinses a 25.00 mL pipette with distilled water and then, without drying it, uses it to transfer the sodium carbonate aliquot into the conical flask. All other steps are carried out correctly. Explain the effect of this on the calculated concentration of the hydrochloric acid." Answer: the water left in the pipette dilutes the aliquot, so it holds fewer moles of carbonate than calculated; less acid is needed, so the titre is smaller; the calculation divides the full calculated moles by a smaller titre, so c(HCl) is too high. Crossed mistake: "the carbonate is diluted, so c(HCl) comes out too low". (A2, Revision 2, the learning review's alternative) "Before adding the aliquot, a student rinses the conical flask with the sodium carbonate solution. All other steps are carried out correctly. Explain the effect of this on the calculated concentration of the hydrochloric acid." Answer: the rinse leaves a film of carbonate solution in the flask, so the flask holds more moles than the aliquot alone; more acid is needed, so the titre is bigger; the calculation divides the aliquot's moles by a bigger titre, so c(HCl) is too low. Crossed mistake: "rinsing with the solution is correct, so no effect". The two answers differ (A1 too high, A2 too low).
teaching.curriculumScope: Syllabus (NSW Chemistry Stage 6, 2017), as printed: "conduct practical investigations to analyse the concentration of an unknown acid or base by titration" this video prepares students to carry out and analyse a titration practical; it does not claim that watching it is conducting it. It teaches: preparing a sodium carbonate primary standard (dried, weighed, dissolved, transferred with rinsings, made up to the mark, inverted) and why each step matters; pipetting the aliquot (rinse with the solution, filler, drain, touch the tip, leave the last drop); why the conical flask may be wet with distilled water; setting up the burette (rinse with the acid, fill below eye level, remove the funnel, fill the tip, no bubble); reading the burette at eye level to 0.05 mL; the rough run and the accurate runs (fast to about 1 mL short, then dropwise with swirling, first permanent orange); the results table, a faulty run identified by its cause, excluded and repeated (the C12 draft correction 2 fix); the calculation in one compact pass (C12 callback); tracing a technique error through the titre to the answer (water-rinsed burette, bubble); controlled conditions; validity, reliability and accuracy, including "concordant is not the same as accurate"; the risk assessment. Placement (playlist order 19): after C12 (order 18), before G03 (order 20) and before C13 (indicators, order 21), C14 (curves), C15 (back and conductometric titrations) and C16 (method choice). So methyl orange is named, with its colours, but not justified (C13 owns indicator choice); no curve, conductivity or back titration appears. Not re-taught: what a titration, standard solution, aliquot, titre, endpoint, equivalence point, primary standard and concordance are; the four-step calculation; why carbonate takes two HCl (all C12; recalled in one clause each). Not here: indicator choice and equivalence pH (chem-m6-c13); error-direction tables across many errors (chem-m6-g04); aliquot scale-up, percentage by mass and the full mass-to-concentration practice (chem-m6-g03); percentage uncertainty arithmetic; boiling out carbon dioxide near the endpoint (author note e).

design.visualSystem: Explainer engine: warm paper stage, handwritten Caveat headings, amber doodle layer. Colour key on screen throughout (C12): the known solution's values (standard) navy; the unknown's values amber; the ratio box teal; concordant titres ringed teal, excluded rows crossed grey; error-chain chips: cause grey, "titre bigger" or "titre smaller" violet, "answer too low" or "too high" terracotta; controls green, hazards terracotta; methyl orange yellow, orange and red as painted. Board layout (three zones, constant, as P05): top-left the short task line; the centre holds the apparatus; the right third holds the current card (procedure step, reason, titre table, calculation, error chain, VRA, risk), one at a time. Clutter rule: at most three bright text items; every tag dims when its sentence ends. Reuse: painted plates, inspected 21 Oct: `m6-burette-clamp-stand-v1.png` (retort stand, clamp, burette with blue tap; the fill gauge drawn over its tube), `m6-conical-flask-v1.png`, `m6-white-tile-v1.png`, `m6-volumetric-flask-v1.png` (stoppered, with a neck mark), `m6-volumetric-pipette-filler-v1.png` (bulb pipette with red filler, native aspect, rotated whole), `m6-funnel-v1.png` (glass funnel; the standard transfer and the burette fill), `m6-beaker-v1.png` (the weighing beaker; the beaker of unknown acid), `m6-wash-bottle-v1.png` (rinses), `m6-indicator-methyl-orange-set-v1.png` (three conical flasks, red, orange and yellow, in one plate; scene 8 thumbnail of the colour order and the fallback for the endpoint flask, see Assets), `m5x-safety-glasses-v1.png` (risk). From P03's Codex asset brief (not yet painted): `m6-buffer-bottle-v1.png` is not needed here. Not used: `m6-clip-phenolphthalein-*` (wrong indicator for this titration), the bench balance clip art in `public/assets/` root (`scale.png`, `lab-footage-balance-beaker.png`: inspected, white-background icon style that does not match the painted plates). No human figures.
